first_impression: Generated Metal per robot, one thread per env, with real fusion numbers. Ambitious for a solo day, I want to look at the kernel.
confusing: Slide 10: '90x = about 4x GPU and ~30x kernel fusion' does not multiply (4x30 is 120), and the headline is 60x, so three numbers conflict
Slide 10: MuJoCo baseline is the stock Python mj_step loop with no batching or multithreaded rollout, which flatters the headline
Slide 5: the kernel excerpt shows only the motor lines, nothing about contacts or the solver
Slide 14: policy transferred to a MuJoCo mirror the author also built, so it is sim-to-sim
doubts: 60x versus MuJoCo is against a deliberately unoptimized baseline; MuJoCo MJX and Warp would be the fair comparison
Slide 9: hard impulses vs soft constraints diverging after 0.6 s means the walker is not very MuJoCo-like
16,384 walkers in 7.6M steps/s vs 4,096 in training at 295K steps/s is a 25x gap you only partly explain
questions: What is your threadgroup size and how much of the step is register-resident versus threadgroup memory?
Does the kernel recompile at 0.24 s via the Metal compiler or a cached pipeline?
How did you get from 7.6M raw to 295K end-to-end, and is the PPO update on the same MLX stream?
Why not compare to MJX or MuJoCo Warp on CPU/Metal?

Label the transfer slide 'sim-to-sim' in the headline so nobody mistakes it for hardware

confusing: Slide 13: 'RL classes on MacBooks' is the wedge but there is no evidence of a single class or user, and the Colab answer is thin
Slide 2 and 6: 'days of experience' counts simulated time, easy to misread as compute saved
Slide 10: the 60x headline vs slide 14's 2D caveat; real RL users want 3D, so the audience for 2D planar is small
Slide 12: '18 checks passing' is vague, what are the checks
doubts: Students want 3D arms and humanoids, not a planar walker; planar 2D may be a toy

first_impression: Unusually good validation for a hackathon: five seeds, MuJoCo comparison, measured transfer. But statistics are thin and some metrics are loosely defined.
confusing: Slide 7: chart metric is average distance per finished training episode (54.9 m) while the lanes show 21.5 m in an 8 s eval; two metrics side by side on one slide
Slide 9: RMS and 'within 5 cm for 0.6 to 0.8 s' are reported without a clear tolerance or a baseline of what MuJoCo vs MuJoCo with another solver would give
Slide 14: n=10 episodes, deterministic policy, nearly identical starts, so 0 falls tells little about robustness
Slide 8: 6.16 vs 2.74 m/s is one run, no seeds or variance
doubts: 5 seeds with ±3.7 m is a small sample and the shaded band has a wide spread between 20 and 40 s
The policy gap 19.8 vs 21.9 m is a 10 percent drop, called transfer success without an error bar or perturbation test
Slide 6 simulated time arithmetic uses steps not accounting for episode resets, so 'experience' is an upper count
Foot-slip metric is the only cheating detector; no ablation showing it catches other exploits
questions: What are the initial-state randomization and the confidence interval on the 10 episode comparison?
Why are contact trajectories divergent, did you tune the impulse parameters to MuJoCo or fit them?
Is there an ablation showing warm-starting alone vs the DC motor curve fixes the cheating?
How did you pick the 0.6 to 0.8 s cutoff and what is the error growth rate?

fixes.change: Show one divergence-over-time curve with a stated tolerance and a MuJoCo-vs-MuJoCo-alternate-solver reference
Add per-episode scatter or standard deviation and randomized initial states for the transfer test, state n
Add an ablation line: foot slip with only warm-start, only DC motor, both
Use the same metric for chart and lanes or label the difference directly on the chart
Note the experience number counts sim time across resets and give the formula inputs on the slide
